problem: ObjectNav and VLN accept only natural-language goals and must explore at test time, so they cannot handle instructions that need commonsense reasoning or an image to resolve the goal, such as 'Where should I return this?' said while holding a bin. Prompting VLMs directly also falls short: short-context VLMs cannot ingest a full environment tour, and robot actions are out of distribution for VLMs.
motivation: A demonstration tour video is cheap to collect (teleoperation or a smartphone walk-through) and matches how people show a new robot around their home. Long-context VLMs such as Gemini 1.5 Pro (1M tokens) can take in a whole high-frame-rate tour together with an interleaved text+image instruction. The authors observe that VLMs reason well about which place in the tour satisfies an instruction but are poor at emitting motor actions, which suggests splitting the problem hierarchically.
key_idea: A long-context VLM reads the entire demonstration tour video plus the multimodal instruction and outputs only a goal frame index. A classical low-level policy then reaches that frame by visual localization and shortest-path planning on a topological graph built offline from the tour with structure-from-motion.
insight: Asking the VLM to select a goal frame, instead of emitting actions, is what makes the system work. In NeRF simulation, prompting Gemini 1.5 Pro for left/forward/right actions gives 0% SR (it almost always says 'forward') at 25.90 s per step. Goal index plus topological graph gives 90% SR, SPL 0.84 and 0.19 s per step. Long context is the second key ingredient: downsampling the tour to 0.2 FPS so it fits GPT-4V/4o drops Gemini's goal finding on Reasoning-Required from 86% to 67% and on Multimodal from 90% to 60%, and GPT-4o/4V cannot take 1 FPS at all. The appendix ablation shows that multimodal instructions need raw images on both sides: a captioned 'text tour' reaches only 20% on MM instructions and captioning the instruction image gives 40%, versus 90% with images. The remaining bottleneck is perception at tour resolution: Small Objects goal finding is 42%, while low-level goal reaching is 100% even with a tour recorded months earlier.
method: MINT task formulation: inputs are a first-person demonstration tour F (frames, optional per-frame narratives N) and a multimodal instruction (text d, optional image I); the policy π(a|O,F,N,d,I) outputs a robot-centric waypoint (Δx, Δy, Δθ).

Offline topological graph: COLMAP SfM estimates a 6-DoF pose for every tour frame; each frame becomes a vertex; a directed edge is added when the target vertex is within 2 m and less than 90° from the source vertex's heading.

High-level goal finding: one interleaved prompt (all tour frames labeled 'Frame i' with narratives, the current camera image as the image instruction, and the user text) is sent to Gemini 1.5 Pro, which returns the integer index g of the closest goal frame; 948 frames at 1 FPS fit in its 1M-token context; one call takes 10–30 s.

Hierarchical visual localization: a DELG-style global descriptor retrieves the k nearest tour frames; local 2D features are matched to the SfM 2D-3D correspondences; PnP gives the pose T and the closest vertex v_s; the SfM scale factor makes waypoints metric; median ATE is 0.056 m; if localization fails it falls back to the last pose.

Low-level goal reaching: at each step, Dijkstra finds the shortest path from v_s to v_g on the graph; the waypoint is the relative pose of the next vertex with respect to T, executed by an iLQR/MPC controller (trajax) that also avoids obstacles; 0.19 s per step.

numbers_note: No standard benchmark is used. All results come from the authors' own MINT evaluation: one real 836 m² office with 57 crowd-sourced instructions, a NeRF simulation of that office, and a small real home-like environment. Split 'test' is nominal. Metric keys are suffixed by instruction category (RF = Reasoning-Free, RR = Reasoning-Required, SO = Small Objects, MM = Multimodal). SPL is printed as a fraction (e.g. 0.59) and converted to 0-100. GoalFindSR is high-level goal-frame accuracy only. The abstract/intro headline '86% and 90%' are the Table 3 goal-finding SRs for RR and MM. The appendix ablation on MM instructions (text tour 0.20, captioned instruction with multimodal tour 0.40, ours 0.90, GPT-4o text tour 0.10) is not listed as separate entries. Baselines (CLIP-based retrieval, Text-Only Mobility VLA) are omitted as instructed.
results: On the real office, Mobility VLA reaches end-to-end SR 80/80/40/85% and SPL 0.59/0.69/0.38/0.64 on RF/RR/SO/MM instructions, with 100% low-level goal reaching. High-level goal finding over all 57 instructions is 95/86/42/90%. It beats the NLMap-style CLIP-retrieval baseline (35/33/25/20%) and a Text-Only captioned-tour variant (70/60/50/30%); the text-only variant does better only on Small Objects (50% vs 42%). In NeRF simulation it achieves 90% SR and SPL 0.84 over 1000 episodes, against 0% for direct VLM action output. A smartphone-recorded home tour yields 100% SR with SPL 0.87.
limitations: Relies on a prior demonstration tour and cannot explore; it can only navigate to places and objects seen in the tour, which assumes a mostly static scene.
High-level Gemini inference takes 10–30 s per query, and the method depends on a closed long-context model; GPT-4V/4o cannot ingest a 1 FPS tour.
Small-object goals fail often (40–42%) because of limited tour resolution. Evaluation is small-scale: one office, 57 instructions, 5 per category in the real-robot runs; sim covers only RF/RR.
builds_on: hierarchical visual localization (global descriptor retrieval + PnP)
compares_to: CLIP-based retrieval (NLMap reproduction with OWL-ViT + CLIP; representative of ESC/ZSON/CoW)
Text-Only Mobility VLA (VLM-captioned text tour + Gemini 1.5 Pro LLM)
